Outliers analysis

Using the df_clean dataframe answer the following questions. Focus on the variables Flipper length and Bill length for all the analyses.

Q2: Use the Local Outlier Factor method (with \(k=20\)) and identify the top five outliers using the quantile \(97.5\%\) tp find the score threshold. Generate a scatter plot to display the dataset, highlighting any observations classified as outliers.**

sum(is.na(df_clean)) #make sure no NAs
## [1] 0
# Select study vars (flipper lenght, bill length)
df_lof <- df_clean[,c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_length_mm")]

# Compute LOF scores k = 20
lof_scores <-lof(df_lof, k=20) #set k to 20
#Set threshold
thr_lof <-quantile(lof_scores, 0.975, type = 7) #type 7 by default 

# Classify outliers according to threshold
df_lof$outlier_lof <-ifelse(lof_scores >= thr_lof, "Outlier", "Normal") 

# Identify Top 5 outliers
top5_idx_lof <-order(lof_scores, decreasing = TRUE) [1:5] #top 2.5% obs LOF score > 9.1 classified as outlier
df_lof$outlier_lof[top5_idx_lof] <- "Top 5 Outliers"

# Do scatter plot
ggplot(df_lof, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
          color = outlier_lof, shape = outlier_lof)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = outlier_lof), alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Normal"         = 19,
                                "Outlier"        = 1,
                                "Top 5 Outliers" = 10)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Normal"         = "grey",
                                "Outlier"        = "blue",
              "Top 5 Outliers" = "blue")) +
  scale_size_manual(values  = c("Normal"         = 4,
              "Outlier"        = 4,
              "Top 5 Outliers" = 4)) +
  labs(title    = "Local Outlier Factor Detection",
       subtitle = paste("Threshold (97.5% quantile):", round(thr_lof, 2)),
       x        = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y        = "Bill Length (mm)",
    color    = "Classification",
    shape    = "Classification",
    size     = "Classification") +
  theme_minimal()

Q3: Use the Isolation Tree algorithm with \(100\) trees and identify the top five outliers. Use the quantile \(97.5\%\) to find the score threshold Generate a scatter plot to display the dataset, highlighting any observations classified as outliers.**

# Select the study vars (flipper lenght, bill length)
df_iso <- df_clean[,c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_length_mm")]

# Train isolation forest 
iso_forest <-isolation.forest(df_iso, ndim=2, ntrees = 100) #set ntrees to 100

# Generate an anomaly score for each obs (between 0 and 1). The closer to 1, the more likely to be an outlier
iso_scores <-predict(iso_forest, df_iso, type = "score")

# Set threshold
thr_iso <-quantile(iso_scores, 0.975, type = 7) #type 7 by default 

# Classify outliers according to threshold
df_iso$outlier_iso <-ifelse(iso_scores >= thr_iso, "Outlier", "Normal") 

# Identify Top 5 outliers
top5_idx_iso <-order(iso_scores, decreasing = TRUE) [1:5] #top 2.5% obs are considered outliers
df_iso$outlier_iso[top5_idx_iso] <- "Top 5 Outliers" 

# Do scatter plot

ggplot(df_iso, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
          color = outlier_iso, shape = outlier_iso)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = outlier_iso), alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Normal"         = 19,
                                "Outlier"        = 1,
                                "Top 5 Outliers" = 13)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Normal"         = "grey",
                                "Outlier"        = "red",
              "Top 5 Outliers" = "red")) +
  scale_size_manual(values  = c("Normal"         = 4,
              "Outlier"        = 4,
              "Top 5 Outliers" = 4)) +
  labs(title    = "Isolation Tree Outlier Detection (ntrees = 100)",
       subtitle = paste("Threshold (97.5% quantile):", round(thr_iso, 2)),
       x        = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y        = "Bill Length (mm)",
    color    = "Classification",
    shape    = "Classification",
    size     = "Classification") +
  theme_minimal()

Q4: From the previous results, which observations can be considered outliers? Why? Discuss what actions should be taken regarding them

“An outlier is an observation which deviates so much from the other observations as to arouse suspicions that it was generated by a different mechanism” - Douglas Hawkins.

To conduct a more accurate comparison between algorithms, we will visualize the “Top 5 outliers” detected by the Isolation Tree and the Local Outlier Factor (LOF) methods. We can state that three in the top five outliers detected, are coincidental in both.

# Combine both methods into one dataframe
df_compare <- df_clean[, c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_length_mm")]
df_compare$lof_class <- df_lof$outlier_lof
df_compare$iso_class <- df_iso$outlier_iso

ggplot(df_compare, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey", size = 4, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = df_compare[df_compare$lof_class == "Top 5 Outliers", ],
             aes(color = "LOF"), size = 4, shape = 3) +
  geom_point(data = df_compare[df_compare$iso_class == "Top 5 Outliers", ],
             aes(color = "Isolation Forest"), size = 4, shape = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("LOF" = "blue", "Isolation Forest" = "red")) +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Outliers: LOF vs Isolation Forest",
       x     = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y     = "Bill Length (mm)",
       color = "Method") +
  theme_minimal()

To determine the appropriate treatment for outliers, we should have more information about the context of the study. Additionally, inspecting the data values highlighted as outliers, might be useful, alongside the mean bill and flipper lengths for these species may be beneficial. Identifying an extreme outlier could indicate an error in data collection or sampling.

Missing values analysis

Now using the df dataframe, answer the following questions:

Q5: Are there missing values? How we classify them (MCAR; MAR; MNAR)? Quantify the quality of the data using the missing values.

There are 19 missing values in the dataset distributed across variables: “bill_depth_mm” (2), “bill_length_mm” (2), “flipper_length_mm” (2), “body_mass_g” (2) and “sex” (11). Given a total number of 3096 observations, the missingness represents only 0,55% of the values, consequently, the dataset is considered to be of high quality.

According to literature, we can classify missing values in three different groups, thus being:

  • MCAR (Missing completely at random): when the missingness is purely a matter of chance.

  • MAR (Missing at Random): the missingness is related to observed data but not the missing values themselves.

  • MNAR (Missing Not at Random): the missingness depends on the unobserved value itself or other unmeasured factors.

## Sum number of NAs in df
cat('Total number of NAs:', sum(is.na(df)), '\n')
## Total number of NAs: 19
(NAs_per_column = data.frame(NAs=colSums(is.na(df))))
## Quality of the data 
#Visualization
vis_miss(df, sort_miss = TRUE) #ggplot of the missingness inside the df

gg_miss_upset(df) #possible intersections bt the variables missingnes

## Classification between MCAR; MAR; MNAR
#MCAR test 
mcar_test(df) #check if the data is in the MCAR category (null hypothesis) p-value = 0.55 > 0.05, we fail to reject H₀ — meaning the data is consistent with MCAR

To categorize the missing data, we conduct an MCAR test with a level of (\(\alpha = 0.05\)). Since the resulting p-value is 0,55 we fail to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the numerical variables are Missing Completely at Random (MCAR).

This means that the missingness is stochastic and unrelated to any other observed variables. Consequently, the NAs we are dealing with can be safely removed or imputed without introducing systematic bias into the model.

Q6: Perform a k-NN Imputation and a MICE imputation. Compare them. Which imputation has better quality? Why?

Hint: I provide code for the plots. Store the k-NN imputation in a dataframe with name df_1nn and the MICE imputation in a dataframe with name df_mice in order to perform the plots. Think carefully your answers and check the consistency of the imputations.

## k-NN and MICE imputations
df_1nn <- kNN(df, k = 1, imp_var=FALSE)
imp_mice <- mice(df, m = 5, printFla=FALSE) #number of default imputations, PARA ENRIQUE: NO SE SI CALDRIA FER-NE DE MES O DE MENYS O FEM TOT BY DEFAULT 
df_mice <-complete(imp_mice)

## Code provided for the plots
plot_columns <- cols[-c(1,6)]

for (column in plot_columns){
  comparison_df <- data.frame(
  KNN_1    = df_1nn[[column]],
  MICE     = df_mice[[column]]
  )
  plot_data <- comparison_df %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Method", values_to = "Value")
  
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Value, color = Method, fill = Method)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.1, linewidth = 1) +
    labs(
      title = "Comparison of Imputation Methods: 
      Distribution of flipper_length_mm",
      x = "Value of flipper_length_mm",
      y = "Density"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1")
  
  print(p)
  
}

subset_knn <- df_1nn %>%
  select(body_mass_g, sex) %>%
  mutate(Method = "kNN")

subset_mice <- df_mice %>%
  select(body_mass_g, sex) %>%
  mutate(Method = "MICE")

df_comparison <- bind_rows(subset_knn, subset_mice)

df_comparison <- df_comparison %>%
  mutate(sex = factor(sex, labels = c("Female", "Male")))

ggplot(df_comparison, aes(x = sex, y = body_mass_g, fill = Method)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ Method) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of Body Mass by Sex across Imputation Methods",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Once the computations are performed, it’s difficult to observe any differences between the results of both imputation methods, as they are almost identical at first sight. Density plots reveal similar shapes, and boxplot show very similar medians and IQRs.

To determine which method produces better results, we must consider their characteristics and properties, according to the methodologies used for computation. Thus being:

  • 1-NN: it only uses values that actually exist in our data so the generating mechanism produces them. It is sensitive to outliers.

  • MICE: it preserves the distribution (mean and variance). It accounts for statistical uncertainty, therefore and shows better performance than 1-NN when working with datasets with higher rates of missingness.

Nonetheless, if we had to choose one method over the other, we would stick with k-NN because the data we are working with has low missingness and low dimensionality. Also, k-NN can handle local groupings (keep in mind we are working with different types of penguin species).

MICE would outperform k-NN if we were working with a much higher missingness ratio and a high-dimensional dataset. However, it is more computationally costly.

Multivariate matrices

Using the data without missing values (complete cases: df_clean) answer the following questions:

Q8: Compute the sample mean vector \(m\), the centering matrix \(H\) and the centered data matrix \(X_c\). Only matrix and vector operations are allowed.

The sample mean vector \(m\) is defined as:

\(\mathbf{m}_{p \times 1} = \frac{1}{n} \left( \mathbf{1}^T X \right)^T\)

The centering matrix \(H\) is defined as:

\(H = I - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1} \mathbf{1}^T\)

To obtain the centered data matrix \(X_c\) we must operate:

\(X_c = X - \mathbf{1}_{n \times 1} m^T = X - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1} \mathbf{1}^T X = \left( I - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1} \mathbf{1}^T \right) X\)

Which can be synthesized as: \(X_c = H X\)

##Previous steps

# Create matrix X
X <-as.matrix(df_clean[, sapply(df_clean, is.numeric)])

# Define terms
nX <- nrow(X) #Number of obs
pX <- ncol(X) #Number of vars
one_n <- matrix(1, nX, 1) #For easier calculations: create vector 1 with n dimensions
I_n <- diag(nX) #For easier computations

## Computation of the sample mean vector m (px1)
m <- (1 / nX) * t(one_n) %*% X

## Computation of the centering matrix H
H <- I_n - (1 / nX) * one_n %*% t(one_n)

## Computation centered data matrix Xc
X_c <- H %*% X
print('Means by column of centered data matrix')

round(apply(X_c, 2, mean), 2)

Q9: Using the centered data matrix compute the sample covariance matrix \(S\). Only matrix and vector operations are allowed.

The sample covariance matrix \(S\) is defined as: \(S = \frac{1}{n-1} X_c^T X_c\)

## Computation of sample covariance matrix S
(S <- (1 / (nX - 1)) * t(X_c) %*% X_c)

Q10: Obtain the standardized data matrix \(X_s\) and use it to compute the sample correlation matrix \(R\). Only matrix and vector operations are allowed.

The standardized data matrix is defined as follows:

\(X_s = X_c D_s^{-1}\)

where \(D_s\) is expressed as: \({diag}(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_p)\); and where \(X_s\) can also be expressed as \(X_s = H X D_s^{-1}\)

The sample correlation matrix \(R\) is defined as:

\(R = D_s^{-1} S D_s^{-1} = \frac{1}{n-1} X_s^T X_s\)

## Previous calculations
#std_devs <- apply(X_c, 2, sd) #sd for each var
D_s <- diag(diag(sqrt(S))) #creation diag matrix Ds
## Warning in sqrt(S): NaNs produced
## Computation of the standardized data matrix Xs
X_s <- X_c %*% solve(D_s) 

print('Sd by column of standardized data matrix')
## [1] "Sd by column of standardized data matrix"
round(apply(X_s, 2, sd), 2)
## [1] 1 1 1 1 1
## Computation of the sample correlation matrix R
#R <- solve(D_s) %*% S %*% solve(D_s)
(R = 1/(nX-1) * t(X_s) %*% X_s)
